checkpoints.title: Determining the Next Hop from the Destination
checkpoints.prompt: A route table contains 10.0.0.0/8 and 10.1.0.0/16, and the destination is 10.1.2.3. Select one correct conclusion.

choices.text: Choose the /16 route.
choices.explanation: Among the routes that match the destination, the /16 route with the longest prefix is preferred.

choices.text: Choose the /8 route that was registered first.
choices.explanation: The priority of matching routes is not determined by registration order.

choices.text: Send traffic to both the /8 and /16 routes.
choices.explanation: When the destination is included in both ranges, the more specific /16 route is selected.

checkpoints.title: Three Architectures for Internet Communication with IPv4
checkpoints.prompt: Allow only outbound requests from an EC2 instance in a private subnet to an external API. Select the two required components.

choices.text: A default route from the private subnet to the NAT gateway
choices.explanation: In the route table associated with the EC2 subnet, send outbound traffic to the NAT gateway.

choices.text: A route from the public subnet containing the NAT gateway to the internet gateway
choices.explanation: A path from the public NAT gateway to the internet is required.

choices.text: Opening all inbound ports from external sources to the EC2 instance
choices.explanation: It is not necessary to open all ports to external sources to receive responses to connections initiated by the EC2 instance.

choices.text: Attaching an internet gateway directly to an EC2 instance in the private subnet
choices.explanation: An internet gateway is attached to the VPC. In this configuration, outbound traffic from the EC2 instance is sent to the NAT gateway.

checkpoints.title: Difference Between Security Groups and Network ACLs
checkpoints.prompt: For EC2 in a VPC, responses to connections that were allowed to be initiated are permitted without adding reverse-direction allow rules. Select one mechanism that behaves this way.

choices.text: Security group
choices.explanation: Security groups are stateful and allow responses to permitted traffic based on connection state.

choices.text: Network ACL
choices.explanation: Network ACLs evaluate inbound and outbound traffic separately by direction.

choices.text: Route table
choices.explanation: Route tables determine where packets are sent; they do not manage connection state.

checkpoints.title: Troubleshooting private connectivity failures step by step
checkpoints.prompt: The private service name returns the correct IP address, and the destination Security Group already allows the traffic. Select one combination to check next.

choices.text: The source security group's outbound rules, the sender's route, the network ACLs of each subnet, and the return route
choices.explanation: Check not only the destination, but also source authorization and the paths in both directions.

choices.text: Delete the DNS record and add a different name.
choices.explanation: The destination name is already resolving correctly.

choices.text: Allow all traffic using only the destination security group.
choices.explanation: If there is a problem with source authorization or the paths in both directions, this action cannot isolate the cause.

choices.text: A destination CIDR or prefix list and the target to which packets are sent
choices.explanation: A route determines where packets matching the specified destination range are sent.

choices.text: Only the ports allowed for inbound traffic by a security group
choices.explanation: Ports allowed for inbound traffic are specified by rules such as security group rules.

choices.text: A rule that resolves a DNS name to a public IP address
choices.explanation: DNS is responsible for name resolution.

finalQuestions.prompt: A network administrator is reviewing a route table associated with a VPC subnet. What does one route entry in the table map? Select one correct answer.
finalQuestions.title: The Role of Routes

choices.text: The destination 10.1.2.3 is within the range of 10.0.0.0/8.
choices.explanation: 10.0.0.0/8 includes IPv4 addresses whose first 8 bits are 10.

choices.text: The destination 10.1.2.3 is also within the range of 10.1.0.0/16.
choices.explanation: 10.1.0.0/16 includes IPv4 addresses whose first two octets are 10.1.

choices.text: Because the range of 10.0.0.0/8 is broader, the route for 10.0.0.0/8 is used.
choices.explanation: Among matching candidates, the /16 route with the narrower target range is preferred.

finalQuestions.prompt: An operations administrator is investigating traffic destined for 10.1.2.3 in a VPC with no other matching routes. When the source route table contains 10.0.0.0/8 and 10.1.0.0/16, select one incorrect statement about route selection.
finalQuestions.title: Longest Prefix Match

choices.text: Check whether the other VPC has a return route to the source CIDR.
choices.explanation: Correct. Bidirectional communication requires a return path.

choices.text: Check whether the route table resolves DNS names.
choices.explanation: Name resolution is the responsibility of DNS.

choices.text: Check the security group and network ACL permissions on both sides.
choices.explanation: Correct. Routes and filters are separate control points.

choices.text: Delete the local route.
choices.explanation: There is no need to delete the local route used for communication within the VPC.

finalQuestions.prompt: A network administrator is investigating an order API that uses VPC peering. The call reaches the other VPC's subnet, but the caller cannot receive the response. Select two correct items for further investigation.
finalQuestions.title: Return Path

choices.text: Add a route to the internet gateway in the subnet's route table.
choices.explanation: A route used for communication with the internet is required.

choices.text: Assign a public IPv4 address or Elastic IP address to EC2.
choices.explanation: This is required to make EC2 directly accessible from the internet over IPv4.

choices.text: Placing a NAT gateway in a private subnet eliminates the need for an internet gateway.
choices.explanation: An internet gateway is required to expose EC2 directly over IPv4 in this configuration.

choices.text: Allow the applicable HTTPS traffic in the security group.
choices.explanation: In addition to configuring the route, allow the required traffic.

choices.text: Even if only a private IPv4 address is assigned to EC2, the internet gateway automatically performs the translation.
choices.explanation: Direct IPv4 communication requires a corresponding public IPv4 address or Elastic IP address on EC2.

finalQuestions.prompt: A web administrator wants to directly accept IPv4 HTTPS connections from users on the internet to EC2 in a VPC. Choose two incorrect explanations of the conditions required for reachability from the internet.
finalQuestions.title: Public IPv4 Address Reachability

choices.text: Initiate a new SSH connection from outside to EC2.
choices.explanation: A NAT gateway can be used for outbound communication initiated from the private subnet side, such as EC2.

choices.text: Use it as the exit point for outbound communication initiated by EC2.
choices.explanation: Correct.

choices.text: Make all security group rules unnecessary.
choices.explanation: NAT does not replace the permission mechanism.

finalQuestions.prompt: An operations administrator wants an EC2 instance without a public IPv4 address to connect to a distribution source on the internet and retrieve update files. Choose one correct use of a public NAT gateway.
finalQuestions.title: NAT Scope

choices.text: Check whether the private subnet's default route points to the NAT gateway.
choices.explanation: A route is required to send packets from EC2 to the NAT gateway.

choices.text: Check whether the public subnet containing the NAT gateway has a route to the internet gateway.
choices.explanation: A route is required for traffic to leave the NAT gateway and reach the internet.

choices.text: Conclude that the NAT gateway has failed solely because it does not respond to ping.
choices.explanation: The NAT gateway itself does not respond to ping. Check its operational status, the routes, and traffic permissions.

finalQuestions.prompt: An operations administrator is investigating why an external API cannot be reached from EC2 in a private subnet through a public NAT gateway deployed per Availability Zone. Choose one incorrect interpretation of the clues.
finalQuestions.title: NAT Routing

choices.text: A Security Group is stateful and allows responses to permitted traffic based on connection state.
choices.explanation: You do not need to add a reverse-direction rule for responses to permitted traffic.

choices.text: A Network ACL is applied at the instance level and tracks connection state.
choices.explanation: A Network ACL is applied at the subnet level and does not track connection state.

choices.text: A Network ACL permits inbound and outbound traffic separately.
choices.explanation: A Network ACL evaluates rules separately for each traffic direction.

choices.text: A Network ACL is not evaluated if a route exists.
choices.explanation: Even when a route determines the destination, whether traffic is allowed is evaluated separately by the Network ACL.

finalQuestions.prompt: An AWS designer selects rules that allow requests and their responses in a VPC. Choose two statements that correctly describe how Security Groups and Network ACLs work.
finalQuestions.title: Security Groups and Network ACLs

choices.text: Check Network ACL rules in both directions in the subnet containing the ALB and the subnet containing EC2.
choices.explanation: Network ACLs are stateless.

choices.text: If the Security Group is stateful, outbound rules in the Network ACL are unnecessary.
choices.explanation: Correct. Network ACLs independently evaluate outbound traffic as well.

choices.text: Consider the return ephemeral ports.
choices.explanation: This is required when designing Network ACLs.

choices.text: Because Network ACLs apply only to EC2, do not inspect the subnet containing the ALB.
choices.explanation: Correct. Network ACLs apply to subnets.

finalQuestions.prompt: A network administrator controls an HTTPS connection between an Application Load Balancer and EC2 in different subnets using Network ACLs. Choose two incorrect statements about the configuration decision.
finalQuestions.title: Network ACLs and Return Traffic

choices.text: Open all Security Group access and then create a route.
choices.explanation: Diagnose by examining the path and each filter without removing controls.

choices.text: Check the route, the Network ACL at the subnet boundary, and the Security Groups applied to the network interface.
choices.explanation: Investigate the path and the two traffic controls separately.

choices.text: Delete the Network ACL and then check the destination.
choices.explanation: Diagnose without destroying evidence through changes.

finalQuestions.prompt: An operations engineer confirmed that the order API in the VPC resolves to the intended IP and that the application on EC2 is listening on port 443. The application still cannot be reached from another subnet. Choose one correct next check.
finalQuestions.title: VPC Troubleshooting Order

choices.text: Verify that resolving the service name returns the private IP address of the VPC endpoint.
choices.explanation: To use the intended endpoint, the name must resolve to that endpoint's address.

choices.text: Because name resolution succeeded, skip checking the route, the source's outbound rules, and the endpoint's security group.
choices.explanation: Even if name resolution succeeds, problems may remain with the route or communication permissions.

choices.text: If a VPC endpoint policy applies, verify that the caller, operation, and target resource are permitted.
choices.explanation: Even when communication is possible, the endpoint policy may deny a required operation.

finalQuestions.prompt: An operations engineer is investigating why AWS services cannot be accessed through an interface VPC endpoint. The service name resolves to the endpoint's private IP address. Select one investigation approach that is incorrect.
finalQuestions.title: Reachability to an Interface VPC Endpoint

choices.text: Place a route to the peer CIDR in the route tables of both VPCs.
choices.explanation: Correct. Creating a VPC peering connection does not automatically add routes to each subnet's route table.

choices.text: The security groups and network ACLs are automatically opened to all traffic.
choices.explanation: Permission settings are not changed automatically.

choices.text: Verify the required security group and network ACL permissions on both sides.
choices.explanation: Correct.

choices.text: A return route is unnecessary.
choices.explanation: Bidirectional communication requires a return path.

finalQuestions.prompt: A designer has approved peering between two VPCs that use nonoverlapping CIDRs and wants to call an internal API in one VPC from an EC2 instance in the other. Select two settings that must be checked before communication.
finalQuestions.title: Checks After Peering

choices.text: Check the security groups, network ACLs, and return path for the source and destination.
choices.explanation: Even after confirming the source route, the cause may remain in rules that permit communication or in the path for responses to return.

choices.text: Because the API name resolves correctly, skip checking the rules that permit communication.
choices.explanation: Resolving the name does not guarantee that a connection can be made on the target port.

choices.text: If a VPC endpoint policy applies, verify that the caller, operation, and target resource are permitted.
choices.explanation: If the policy denies a required operation, the call fails even when the route to the destination and communication permissions are correct.

choices.text: Until the investigation is complete, open communication from all security groups to all addresses.
choices.explanation: Even a temporary change violates the condition that communication be limited to the required peer and port.

finalQuestions.prompt: A client cannot connect to an internal API in another VPC. The operations engineer has confirmed that the API name returns the correct private IP address and that the source subnet's route is correct. During the investigation, communication must remain limited to the required peer and port. Under these conditions, select two incorrect actions.
finalQuestions.title: Troubleshooting Cross-VPC Connectivity

blocks.label: Overview
blocks.text: Determine the route that matches the destination, then examine in order the path to the internet and the rules that allow communication.

blocks.label: Learning objective
blocks.text: Verify, with supporting evidence, the route, source and destination permissions, and return traffic for communication within and outside a VPC.

blocks.label: Learning objectives
blocks.text: Determine which route is selected based on the destination IP address and longest-prefix match.

blocks.label: Learning objectives
blocks.text: Distinguish the traffic targeted by and the placement of an IGW and a NAT gateway.

blocks.label: Learning objectives
blocks.text: Explain the scope of security groups and network ACLs, and the conditions required to return a response.

blocks.label: Learning objectives
blocks.text: When connectivity within or between VPCs is unavailable, verify name resolution, the round-trip path, and the rules that allow traffic.

blocks.label: Determine the next forwarding destination from the destination
blocks.text: A VPC route table maps destination CIDRs or prefix lists to targets, which are the next forwarding destinations. The initial route table contains a local route used for traffic within the VPC. To communicate with a VPC peer, add a route whose destination is the peer’s address range.

blocks.label: Determine the next forwarding destination from the destination
blocks.text: When multiple routes match, the longest prefix match—that is, the most specific CIDR—is selected. For 10.1.2.3, 10.1.0.0/16 takes precedence over 10.0.0.0/8.

blocks.label: Determine the next forwarding destination from the destination
blocks.text: A one-way route alone cannot establish bidirectional communication such as TCP. For VPC peering, VPNs, and separate VPCs, also check the route back from the peer to the source.

steps.label: Determine the next forwarding destination from the destination

blocks.label: Situation
blocks.text: An EC2 instance in 10.0.2.0/24 cannot connect to 10.1.0.10 on the VPC peering connection.

blocks.label: Step 1
blocks.text: In the source subnet’s route table, verify the target that matches 10.1.0.10.

blocks.label: Step 2
blocks.text: In the peer VPC, verify the route back to 10.0.2.0/24.

blocks.label: Step 3
blocks.text: Check the permissions on both sides and the destination service.

blocks.label: Conclusion
blocks.text: You can diagnose the issue based on the destination and return CIDRs without relying only on the default route.

blocks.label: This is incorrect
blocks.text: If 0.0.0.0/0 exists, any private CIDR can always be reached.

blocks.label: Correction
blocks.text: The target of the default route may not know that private CIDR. You need a target appropriate for the destination and a round-trip path.

blocks.label: Key point
blocks.text: Choose the most specific route for the destination IP.

blocks.label: Key point
blocks.text: The return route is also a communication requirement.

blocks.label: Three Architectures for Internet Communication with IPv4
blocks.text: The diagram first compares which side opens the connection and where a public IPv4 address is required. In an architecture that connects directly to EC2 from outside, provide a public IPv4 address, a route from the subnet to the internet gateway (IGW), and permission for the required ports.

blocks.label: Three Architectures for Internet Communication with IPv4
blocks.text: When EC2 in a private subnet retrieves update files, EC2 initiates the communication. The private subnet’s route points to a public NAT gateway, and the route in the subnet containing the NAT points to the IGW. Assign an Elastic IP to the public NAT.

steps.label: Three Architectures for Internet Communication with IPv4

blocks.label: Three Architectures for Internet Communication with IPv4
blocks.text: In an architecture that provides a service without exposing EC2, users connect to an internet-facing ALB. The ALB terminates that connection and opens a separate connection within the VPC to EC2 in the private subnet. EC2 does not need a public IPv4 address.

steps.label: Three Architectures for Internet Communication with IPv4

blocks.label: Situation
blocks.text: In an architecture using a zonal public NAT gateway, EC2 in a private subnet cannot connect to the OS update destination.

blocks.label: Step 1
blocks.text: Confirm that 0.0.0.0/0 in the private subnet targets the NAT gateway.

blocks.label: Step 2
blocks.text: Confirm that the NAT gateway is in a public subnet and that 0.0.0.0/0 in that subnet targets the IGW.

blocks.label: Step 3
blocks.text: Check EC2’s outbound rules, as well as any NACLs or external-side conditions that could block return traffic.

blocks.label: Conclusion
blocks.text: Rather than stopping after creating the NAT, you can verify the initiating side, the route, and external reachability together.

blocks.label: This is incorrect
blocks.text: If you create a NAT gateway in a private subnet, you can SSH to EC2 in that subnet from outside.

blocks.label: Correction
blocks.text: NAT is an egress path for connections initiated from the private side. It is not intended to relay new inbound connections from outside to private EC2.

blocks.label: Key point
blocks.text: NAT is an egress path for traffic initiated from the private side.

blocks.label: Key point
blocks.text: Check the two routes: private subnet → NAT → IGW.

blocks.label: Differences Between Security Groups and Network ACLs
blocks.text: The diagram compares the boundaries and ports through which requests and responses pass, using an HTTPS connection from an ALB to EC2 as an example. A security group (SG) is applied to a network interface and allows responses to permitted connections.

blocks.label: Differences Between Security Groups and Network ACLs
blocks.text: A network ACL (NACL) is applied to a subnet. It does not track connection state and evaluates inbound and outbound traffic separately. In the diagram, the request travels from the ALB side to TCP 443, and the response returns to TCP 49152, which the ALB used as the source port.

blocks.label: Differences Between Security Groups and Network ACLs
blocks.text: Routes determine where traffic is sent. Allow traffic in both directions with the NACL, while restricting the peer and port for newly initiated connections in the SG. If the connection fails, check which rules apply in which direction.

steps.label: Differences Between Security Groups and Network ACLs

blocks.label: Situation
blocks.text: The HTTPS request from the ALB reaches the web EC2 instance, but the response does not return.

blocks.label: Step 1
blocks.text: Check both directions—the request and the return traffic—in the NACLs for the ALB subnet and the EC2 subnet.

blocks.label: Step 2
blocks.text: In the EC2 security group, allow TCP 443 from the ALB security group.

blocks.label: Step 3
blocks.text: Check the routes for the source and destination, as well as the service listener.

blocks.label: Conclusion
blocks.text: Explain why the NACL outbound rule cannot be omitted even when the security group is stateful.

blocks.label: This is incorrect
blocks.text: If the security group is stateful, the NACL on the same path automatically allows the return traffic.

blocks.label: Correction
blocks.text: An NACL is a stateless filter independent of the security group. NACL rules are required in both directions.

blocks.label: Takeaway
blocks.text: An SG is stateful at the network-interface boundary.

blocks.label: Takeaway
blocks.text: An NACL is stateless at the subnet boundary.

blocks.label: Troubleshooting private connection failures in order
blocks.text: When connecting to a destination through a VPC endpoint or VPC peering, first check whether the name resolves to the intended private IP address. If it resolves to a different IP address, examining the routes or allow rules will not verify the intended path.

blocks.label: Troubleshooting private connection failures in order
blocks.text: Next, check the route of the source subnet, the rules on the sending and receiving sides, and the port on which the destination is listening. If the VPC endpoint has a policy, also check whether the calling principal, operation, and target resource are allowed.

blocks.label: Troubleshooting private connection failures in order
blocks.text: Finally, verify the route for the response to return from the destination to the source and the reverse-direction rules of the network ACL. Record separately whether name resolution succeeds and whether an actual connection can be established.

steps.label: Troubleshooting private connection failures in order

blocks.label: Situation
blocks.text: An application cannot connect from EC2 to an AWS service through an interface VPC endpoint.

blocks.label: Step 1
blocks.text: Confirm that the service name resolves to the endpoint's private IP address.

blocks.label: Step 2
blocks.text: Check the source route and security group, the network ACLs along the path, and the permissions on the endpoint side.

blocks.label: Step 3
blocks.text: Confirm that the endpoint policy allows the caller and the operation, then reconnect under the same conditions.

blocks.label: Conclusion
blocks.text: By checking, in order, the rules that deny name resolution, routing, and connectivity, you can narrow down the cause of the connection failure.

blocks.label: This is incorrect
blocks.text: Creating VPC peering automatically allows all traffic between both VPCs.

blocks.label: Correction
blocks.text: Even after creating VPC peering, verify the routes, security groups, NACLs, and, if necessary, name resolution settings on both sides.

blocks.label: Key point
blocks.text: DNS results are a prerequisite for the route to the destination.

blocks.label: Key point
blocks.text: Do not forget source authorization and return traffic.
